definitions.quantity: Standard Gibbs free energy of binding, ΔG_bind°
definitions.formal_definition: For the association P + L ⇌ PL, ΔG_bind° = −RT ln K° where K° is the standard equilibrium constant. IUPAC Gold Book S05915 defines the standard equilibrium constant verbatim as: 'Quantity defined by K⚬ = e^(−Δ_rG⚬/RT) where Δ_rG⚬ is the standard reaction Gibbs energy, R the gas constant and T the thermodynamic temperature.' Inverting: Δ_rG° = −RT ln K°. For binding, K° = Ka·c° = c°/Kd, so ΔG_bind° = −RT ln(Ka·c°) = +RT ln(Kd/c°). It is a state function of the equilibrium alone: it is fully determined by the position of the P+L⇌PL equilibrium under standard conditions and by nothing else.
definitions.units: kcal/mol (or kJ/mol). Verified this session: R = 8.314462618 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (NIST CODATA 2022, stated exact); with 1 thermochemical cal = 4.184 J, R = 1.987204×10⁻³ kcal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and RT(298.15 K) = 0.592485 kcal/mol. This reproduces platform/cbc/thermo.py RT = 0.59248 to all printed digits.
definitions.sign_convention: NEGATIVE for favourable binding. Kd < 1 M ⇒ ln(Kd/c°) < 0 ⇒ ΔG_bind° < 0. Computed this session with thermo.py's relation: Kd = 1 nM → −12.278; Kd = 5 nM → −11.325; Kd = 1274 nM → −8.042 kcal/mol. The sign is not a convention that may be flipped for display: it is fixed by ΔG° = −RT ln K° and by the second law (spontaneous association at standard state ⇒ ΔG° < 0).
definitions.standard_state: REQUIRED. c° = 1 mol/dm³ for solutes. IUPAC Gold Book S05909 'standard concentration': 'Chosen value of amount concentration denoted by c⚬ and usually equal to 1 mol dm⁻³.' Gold Book S05925 'standard state' for a solute: 'the (hypothetical) state of solute at the standard molality m⚬, standard pressure p⚬ or standard concentration c⚬ and exhibiting infinitely dilute solution behaviour.' Temperature must also be stated; ΔG° is not temperature-independent.
definitions.depends_on_assay_conditions: NO — this is the defining property. ΔG_bind° depends only on P, L, solvent, T, p and ionic conditions defining the equilibrium. It does not depend on substrate concentration, radioligand concentration, enzyme concentration, readout, or incubation time. Any quantity that moves when [S] or [radioligand] is changed is, by that fact alone, not ΔG_bind°.
definitions.source: IUPAC Compendium of Chemical Terminology 5th ed., 'standard equilibrium constant' S05915 (https://doi.org/10.1351/goldbook.S05915), 'standard concentration' S05909, 'standard state' S05925 — all scraped this session. R from NIST CODATA 2022 (https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?r).

definitions.quantity: Dissociation constant Kd, and the relation ΔG° = −RT ln(Ka) = +RT ln(Kd)
definitions.formal_definition: Kd = [P][L]/[PL] at equilibrium for the 1:1 reaction PL ⇌ P + L; Ka = 1/Kd. IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY, verbatim: 'Kd refers to the equilibrium dissociation constant of a ligand determined directly in a binding assay using a labeled form of the ligand.' Strictly, the dimensionless argument of the logarithm is Kd/c°, so ΔG_bind° = +RT ln(Kd/c°) = −RT ln(Ka·c°). Because Kd and ΔG° are related by an invertible function at fixed T, they carry exactly ONE degree of freedom between them — reporting both is one number, not two, and only meaningful when one is declared the transform of the other.
definitions.units: Kd: molar (M, mM, µM, nM, pM). Ka: M⁻¹. Both Kd/c° and Ka·c° are dimensionless.
definitions.sign_convention: Kd is strictly positive. Its logarithm carries the sign: Kd < 1 M ⇒ ΔG° < 0. One decade of Kd = RT·ln(10) = 1.364247 kcal/mol at 298.15 K (computed this session).
definitions.standard_state: c° = 1 M. Kd itself is a concentration and needs no standard state; ΔG° derived from it does. See the separate 'standard state' entry for what changing c° does to the number.
definitions.depends_on_assay_conditions: NO in principle (it is a thermodynamic constant at fixed T, p, buffer, ionic strength); YES in practice for the reported value, because a measured Kd is contaminated by ligand depletion when [P] is not ≪ Kd, by non-equilibrium if incubation is too short, and by buffer/temperature differences. These are measurement errors around a well-defined quantity, categorically unlike IC50's structural dependence on [S].
definitions.source: IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY help page (https://www.guidetopharmacology.org/helpPage.jsp), scraped this session; Gold Book S05915 for the ΔG°/K° relation.

definitions.formal_definition: IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY, verbatim: 'Ki refers to the equilibrium dissociation constant of a ligand determined in inhibition studies. The Ki for a given ligand is typically (but not necessarily) determined in a competitive radioligand binding study by measuring the inhibition of the binding of a reference radioligand by the competing ligand of interest under equilibrium conditions.' Ross et al. 2023, verbatim: 'By definition, the Ki is the Kd of an enzyme inhibitor. However, these quantities differ subtly in the way they are measured; Kis are typically measured in functional enzymatic inhibition assays whereas Kds come from experiments that more directly measure binding.' Formally, for competitive inhibition with E + I ⇌ EI, Ki = k₋i/ki = [E][I]/[EI] (Cer et al. 2009, definitions accompanying Eq. 1a).
definitions.sign_convention: Strictly positive. Enters energy via ΔG° = +RT ln(Ki/c°), negative for potent inhibitors — same convention as Kd.
definitions.standard_state: c° = 1 M when converted to a free energy. Ki itself is a concentration.
definitions.depends_on_assay_conditions: NO by construction — Ki is defined as the substrate-independent quantity that IC50 is corrected TO. Cer et al. 2009, verbatim: 'What is required is an accurate determination of the Ki value, an intrinsic, thermo-dynamic quantity that is independent of the substrate (ligand) but depends on the enzyme (target) and inhibitor.' Caveat: this holds only under the stated mechanism. Ki is mechanism-dependent (competitive vs uncompetitive vs noncompetitive give different Ki from the same IC50), and for tight-binding inhibitors the classical relations fail and Copeland/Henderson corrections are required.
definitions.source: IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY help page; Cer RZ, Mudunuri U, Stephens R, Lebeda FJ, Nucleic Acids Res 37:W441–W445 (2009), PMC2703898, scraped this session; Ross GA et al., Commun Chem 6 (2023), doi 10.1038/s42004-023-01019-9, scraped this session.

definitions.quantity: IC50, and the Cheng–Prusoff relation to Ki
definitions.formal_definition: IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY, verbatim: 'IC50: This term is used in a number of ways: (i) the molar concentration of an antagonist that reduces the response to an agonist by 50%; the concentration of agonist should be given; (ii) the molar concentration of an unlabeled agonist or antagonist that inhibits the binding of a radioligand by 50%; the concentration of radioligand should be given; (iii) the molar concentration of an inhibitory agonist that reduces a response by 50% of the maximal inhibition that can be attained; this latter usage is not recommended-instead the term, EC50, should be used since this is an agonist effect.' Note the definition itself is threefold and each branch carries a mandatory co-reported concentration. CHENG–PRUSOFF, enzyme/substrate, competitive inhibition, retrieved verbatim from two independent open-access sources this session: 'KI = IC50/(1 + ([S]/KM))' (PMC11790956, Nat Commun Chem 2025) and 'Ki = IC50/[1+ [S]/Km)' (PMC11198849, PLoS ONE 2024, bracket typo in original). Equivalently IC50 = Ki·(1 + [S]/Km). CHENG–PRUSOFF, radioligand-displacement form, retrieved verbatim: 'Ki = IC50/[1 + ([L]/Kd)], where [L] and Kd are the concentration and binding affinity of the radiolabeled ligand in the assay' (PMC11915030, ACS 2025).
definitions.units: molar. Same units as Ki; the two differ by the dimensionless factor (1 + [S]/Km).
definitions.standard_state: None applies to IC50 itself — it is not a thermodynamic constant and admits no standard state. A standard state is only introduced illegitimately, by pretending IC50 is a Kd.
definitions.depends_on_assay_conditions: YES, STRUCTURALLY AND UNBOUNDEDLY. IC50 scales with (1 + [S]/Km) for competitive inhibition, so the same inhibitor and the same enzyme give a different IC50 in every assay that uses a different substrate concentration. It also depends on the inhibition mechanism (the uncompetitive and noncompetitive forms are different equations, Cer et al. Eqs. 2a and 3a), on [E] for tight binders, and on the readout. Ross et al. 2023, verbatim: 'Although IC50s are dependent on the concentrations of the protein and ligand as well as the reaction Michaelis constant, under common assay conditions and reaction mechanisms (but not all), the ratio of the IC50s of two ligands is equivalent to the ratios of the Kis.' Note carefully that this rescues only the RATIO, never the absolute value. Cer et al. add the general caveat, verbatim: 'Comparison of Km or IC50 values for a set of inhibitor candidates is only assumed to be valid when they are evaluated under identical experimental conditions.'
definitions.source: IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY help page; PMC11790956; PMC11198849; PMC11915030 (all Europe PMC full text, fetched this session); Cer et al. PMC2703898; Ross et al. doi 10.1038/s42004-023-01019-9. Original: Cheng Y, Prusoff WH, Biochem Pharmacol 22:3099–3108 (1973), PMID 4202581 (PubMed record fetched; no abstract available, equation taken from the secondary sources above).

definitions.formal_definition: IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY, verbatim: 'EC50: The molar concentration of an agonist that produces 50% of the maximal possible effect of that agonist. Other percentage values (EC20, EC40, etc.) can be specified. The action of the agonist may be stimulatory or inhibitory.' It is a potency parameter of a concentration–response curve, not an occupancy constant. EC50 equals the agonist Kd only in the absence of receptor reserve and with a linear stimulus–response coupling — conditions that are the exception, not the rule.
definitions.standard_state: None applies. EC50 is not a thermodynamic constant.
definitions.depends_on_assay_conditions: YES, and more severely than IC50. EC50 depends on receptor expression level (receptor reserve/spare receptors), on amplification in the signalling cascade, on the cell line, on the readout chosen and on the time point. Two labs can obtain EC50 values orders of magnitude apart for the same agonist–receptor pair with no measurement error, because they are measuring different systems. There is no Cheng–Prusoff-style correction that recovers a Kd from an EC50 in general.
definitions.source: IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY help page (scraped this session). The receptor-reserve/amplification qualifications above are standard pharmacology and were NOT retrieved verbatim from a source this session — treat that sentence as expert commentary, not transcription.

definitions.formal_definition: NOT RETRIEVED as a standalone formal definition. What WAS retrieved: ChEMBL Interface Documentation, verbatim: 'if an assay is deposited as a "confirmatory" assay (defined as an assay where a range of SID concentrations have been tested, with a view to determining a measurement of potency), then one of the result types must be marked up as an "Active Concentration" (AC) result type… The AC result type is the calculated potency measurement from the data, and is typically an IC50, EC50, AC50, GI50 or Ki.' So AC50 is a PubChem/HTS 'active concentration' endpoint — the concentration giving 50% of the fitted activity response — but its physical meaning is set by whatever the depositing assay measured, which is not constrained. I decline to reconstruct a tighter definition from memory.
definitions.depends_on_assay_conditions: YES, and the dependence is not even characterisable in general, because AC50 is a container term for whatever concentration–response endpoint an HTS depositor fitted. This is strictly worse than IC50: with IC50 you at least know which correction equation you would need.
definitions.source: ChEMBL Interface Documentation, 'Assay and Activity Questions' (https://chembl.gitbook.io/chembl-interface-documentation/frequently-asked-questions/chembl-data-questions), scraped this session.

definitions.formal_definition: NOT RETRIEVED as a standalone formal definition. ChEMBL states, verbatim, that it keeps no such list: 'Is there a list of all the Activity Types in ChEMBL? No, we do not keep a list of activity or target types.' XC50 appears in ChEMBL only as a member of the pChEMBL-eligible set. ChEMBL Interface Documentation, verbatim: 'pChEMBL is defined as: -Log(molar IC50, XC50, EC50, AC50, Ki, Kd or Potency)', introduced so that 'a number of roughly comparable measures of half-maximal response concentration/potency/affinity [can] be compared on a negative logarithmic scale.' Papadatos et al. 2015 uses the same grouping, verbatim: 'the calculation of the pChEMBL value (the negative logarithm of the activity values (in M units)) for records with dose–response activity types, such as IC50, XC50, EC50, AC50, Ki, Kd, and Potency'. XC50 is in practice the generic 'x'C50 placeholder used when a depositor did not commit to IC50 vs EC50. Note ChEMBL's own hedge: 'roughly comparable', not equal.
definitions.depends_on_assay_conditions: YES, and maximally so — XC50 is definitionally agnostic about which half-maximal endpoint was measured, so it inherits the union of IC50's and EC50's condition dependencies without telling you which applies.
definitions.source: ChEMBL Interface Documentation FAQ (scraped this session); Papadatos G et al., 'Activity, assay and target data curation and quality in the ChEMBL database', PMC4607714 (Europe PMC full text, fetched this session).

definitions.formal_definition: IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY, verbatim: 'pIC50: The negative logarithm to base 10 of the IC50 of an agonist or antagonist.' i.e. pIC50 = −log10(IC50 in mol/L). For the Boltz-2 output y = log10(IC50/µM), pIC50 = 6 − y identically; verified numerically this session for y = 0.10516: 6 − y = 5.8948 and −log10(1.274×10⁻⁶ M) = 5.8948.
definitions.units: Dimensionless (a logarithm of a molar concentration, with the 1 M reference implicit in taking log of a value expressed in M).
definitions.sign_convention: Larger = more potent. Positive for IC50 < 1 M.
definitions.standard_state: Implicitly 1 M, because the concentration is expressed in mol/L before the logarithm — but this is a units convention, not a thermodynamic standard state, because IC50 is not an equilibrium constant.
definitions.depends_on_assay_conditions: YES — pIC50 inherits every dependency of IC50 exactly, shifted onto a log scale. Taking a logarithm converts a multiplicative assay factor into an ADDITIVE OFFSET; it does not remove it. This is the whole mechanism behind Boltz-2's pooling argument and the whole reason that argument does not license absolute values.
definitions.source: IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY help page (scraped this session).

definitions.formal_definition: IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY, verbatim: 'pKi: The negative logarithm to base 10 of the Ki' and 'pKd: The negative logarithm to base 10 of the Kd.' pKd is the only member of this family that maps cleanly onto thermodynamics: ΔG_bind° = −RT·ln(10)·pKd = −1.364247 × pKd kcal/mol at 298.15 K.
definitions.sign_convention: Larger = tighter. ΔG_bind° = −1.364·pKd, so large positive pKd ⇒ large negative ΔG°.
definitions.standard_state: 1 M, implicit in expressing Kd in mol/L before the logarithm — and here it IS a genuine thermodynamic standard state, because Kd is an equilibrium constant.
definitions.depends_on_assay_conditions: NO in principle (same as Kd/Ki). In practice, public pKi data carry substantial inter-laboratory scatter: Ross et al. 2023 reporting Kramer et al. 2012, verbatim: 'They found that the root-mean-square difference between these independent measurements ranged from 0.56 pKi units (0.77 kcal mol⁻¹) to 0.69 pKi units (0.95 kcal mol⁻¹) depending on how the data was curated.' This is the empirical noise floor for ANY method benchmarked against public affinity data.
definitions.source: IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY help page; Ross GA et al., Commun Chem 6 (2023), doi 10.1038/s42004-023-01019-9 (both fetched this session).

definitions.quantity: Why a 1 M standard state is required, and what changes if you pick another
definitions.formal_definition: ΔG° = −RT ln K° requires K° to be DIMENSIONLESS, because you cannot take the logarithm of a quantity with units. For P + L ⇌ PL the concentration quotient [PL]/([P][L]) has units of M⁻¹, so it must be divided through by the standard concentration: K° = Ka·c° = c°/Kd. The standard state is not decoration — it is what makes ΔG° a number at all. Consequently ΔG° also fixes a reference: it is the free energy change on forming one mole of complex from reactants each held at c°.  EFFECT OF CHANGING c°: ΔG°(c°) = RT ln(Kd/c°), so ΔG°(c°₂) − ΔG°(c°₁) = RT ln(c°₁/c°₂). Choosing c° = 1 mM instead of 1 M shifts every binding free energy by RT·ln(1000) = +4.093 kcal/mol at 298.15 K (computed this session as 3 × RT·ln10 = 3 × 1.364247), turning a −12.28 kcal/mol nanomolar binder into −8.19. Nothing physical changed; the number did. This is precisely why an unlabelled 'ΔG' with no standard state and no temperature is not a scientific claim, and why the ONLY differences that survive a change of standard state are differences between two binders at the same c° (the ΔΔG), since the RT ln(c°₁/c°₂) term cancels.
definitions.units: c° in mol/dm³; the resulting ΔG° in kcal/mol or kJ/mol.
definitions.sign_convention: n/a — but note the shift is signed and one-directional: a more dilute standard state makes every binding free energy less negative.
definitions.standard_state: IUPAC Gold Book S05909, verbatim: 'Chosen value of amount concentration denoted by c⚬ and usually equal to 1 mol dm⁻³.' Gold Book S05925 adds that the solute standard state is 'the (hypothetical) state of solute at the standard molality m⚬, standard pressure p⚬ or standard concentration c⚬ and exhibiting infinitely dilute solution behaviour' — note 'hypothetical' and 'infinitely dilute': the 1 M solute standard state is a mathematical extrapolation, not a beaker of 1 M protein.
definitions.depends_on_assay_conditions: NO — but it IS a convention, and it must be declared. An undeclared standard state is an undeclared additive constant.
definitions.source: IUPAC Gold Book S05909 and S05925 (scraped this session); shift computed this session from R = 8.314462618 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (NIST CODATA 2022).

thermodynamics.the_ruling:
THE PRIOR PANEL WAS RIGHT. Its prohibition was scientifically correct, and if it errs it errs on the side of being TOO WEAK IN SCOPE, not too strong. I would uphold it, broaden it, and re-rank its reasons.

=== WHAT THE BOLTZ-2 AFFINITY HEAD ACTUALLY PREDICTS (decisive; all quotes retrieved from the Boltz-2 preprint PDF this session, doi 10.1101/2025.06.14.659707) ===

Training label, verbatim: "For the binding affinity regression values (e.g., Ki, Kd, IC50, AC50, EC50, XC50), we gather data from PubChem, ChEMBL, and BindingDB… All affinity values are standardized to log 10 scale derived from values measured in µM."

Pooling, verbatim, and this is the sentence the entire ruling turns on: "We observed best performance when training a single affinity value head on all available affinity measurements (eg. Ki, Kd, IC50, AC50, EC50, and XC50). Although these metrics reflect different underlying biochemical quantities, Kis and IC50s are related through the Cheng–Prusoff equation, and when comparing affinity values within the same assay, the pairwise differences loss effectively cancel out the correction term, and assays can be combined Ross et al. [2023]."

Curation filter, verbatim: "Filter to affinity measurements with standard type in {'Ki', 'Kd', 'IC50', 'XC50', 'EC50', 'AC50'}."

Loss, verbatim: "Continuous values are supervised using a Huber loss applied to both absolute affinity values and, with stronger weight, to the pairwise intra-assay differences… Binary classification is supervised using a focal loss."

So: ONE head, SIX physically distinct endpoint types, mapped onto a single log10-µM axis, with the regression loss deliberately weighted toward WITHIN-ASSAY DIFFERENCES. The label is pooled. The output therefore has no single physical referent — it is a learned, assay-blended log-potency.

Three further pieces of evidence, all retrieved, that the authors themselves do not treat the absolute value as physical:
(1) Their own metric protocol, verbatim: "For PMAE, MAE, and PW, we additionally report a centered version in which the predicted affinity values for each assay are translated to have the same mean as the corresponding ground truth values." A per-assay mean shift is subtracted before scoring. You do not need to remove an offset from a state function.
(2) Their ensembling, verbatim: "we apply a calibrated ensembling strategy… ŷ = C0·(y1 + y2) + C1·MW_binder + C2, where… C0, C1, and C2 are fitted in the holdout validation set and MW_binder is the molecular weight of the binding s[pecies]." A molecular-weight regression term is bolted onto the prediction. Nothing that admits a fitted MW term is a Gibbs energy.
(3) Their own TYK2 figure plots the "Boltz-2 Screen Score" AGAINST "ABFE readout (kcal/mol) ΔG" as two different axes with |R| = 0.74. The paper treats ΔG as the external reference the score is compared to, never as what the score is. The paper never calls the affinity head output a binding free energy.
(4) Their Limitations section concedes, verbatim: "we notice in Figures 12-14 that the performance varies strongly between assays."

The cited justification, Ross et al. 2023 (Commun Chem 6, doi 10.1038/s42004-023-01019-9), retrieved this session, says verbatim: "Although IC50s are dependent on the concentrations of the protein and ligand as well as the reaction Michaelis constant, under common assay conditions and reaction mechanisms (but not all), the ratio of the IC50s of two ligands is equivalent to the ratios of the Kis." That licenses RATIOS. Boltz-2's own citation supports only within-assay differences. It does not support the absolute level, and Boltz-2 does not claim it does. The platform's error was reading a within-assay-difference license as an absolute-value license.

ChEMBL, whose pooling convention this mirrors, hedges in exactly the same place, verbatim: pChEMBL "allows a number of ROUGHLY COMPARABLE measures of half-maximal response concentration/potency/affinity to be compared on a negative logarithmic scale" (emphasis mine). Roughly comparable is not identical, and ChEMBL's own curation paper warns, verbatim: "users should therefore consider the assay annotation provided in ChEMBL as a filter to remove assays that are clearly not comparable, rather than a guarantee that two assays are comparable."

=== 1. SIGN ===
Name it exactly: the docs' quantity is pIC50 EXPRESSED IN ENERGY UNITS — literally RT·ln(10) × pIC50. The Boltz docs themselves say so, verbatim: "To convert model output to pIC50 in kcal/mol: (6 - y) * 1.364". They say pIC50, not ΔG. The mislabel is the platform's, not the documentation's.

It is NOT |ΔG|. It is numerically −ΔG_bind° (equivalently the standard Gibbs energy of DISSOCIATION, Δ_dissG° = −RT ln(Kd/c°)) under the counterfactual substitution IC50 → Kd. The distinction from |ΔG| is sharp and testable: for a hypothetical IC50 > 1 M the docs' expression goes NEGATIVE, whereas |ΔG| cannot. So it tracks −ΔG, not |ΔG|.

Verified this session on the actual run: y = 0.10515693 ⇒ (6 − y)·1.364 = +8.0406, while thermo.py's kd_to_dg(1.274×10⁻⁶) = −8.042. Same magnitude, opposite sign, agreeing to 0.001 kcal/mol (the residual is the docs' rounding of 1.364247 to 1.364). At 1 nM: +12.276 vs −12.278.

CRITICAL WARNING, and this is why sign must be the LAST argument and not the first: a sign flip is a one-character repair. If the platform "fixes" this by negating and then writes the result into a field called binding_free_energy, it has repaired the least important defect and left the fatal one untouched. The panel's own reasoning led with the sign; that ordering invites exactly this false repair. Note also the operational consequence the panel correctly spotted: fed to thermo.check() unflipped, the dG < −18.3 implausibility guard can never fire, so an arbitrarily absurd prediction passes silently.

=== 2. IDENTITY ===
IC50 ≠ Kd. Not approximately, not usually — structurally.

IC50 → Ki requires Cheng–Prusoff. Retrieved verbatim (PMC11790956): "KI = IC50/(1 + ([S]/KM))"; radioligand form, verbatim (PMC11915030): "Ki = IC50/[1 + ([L]/Kd)]". Conditions: 1:1 stoichiometry, no cooperativity, true equilibrium, correct mechanism identified (the uncompetitive and noncompetitive forms are DIFFERENT equations), classical non-tight-binding kinetics with [I] ≫ [E], and [S] and Km both known. Ki → Kd requires the additional condition that the inhibition assay is reporting the same equilibrium as a direct binding assay — Ross et al., verbatim: "By definition, the Ki is the Kd of an enzyme inhibitor. However, these quantities differ subtly in the way they are measured."

QUANTIFIED ERROR at [S] = Km, competitive inhibitor: IC50/Ki = 1 + [S]/Km = 2 exactly. That is 0.3010 log10 units, and 0.4107 kcal/mol at 298.15 K (computed this session as RT·ln2 = 0.592485 × 0.693147). At [S] = 3Km the factor is 4 → 0.6021 log10 → 0.8214 kcal/mol. At [S] = 10Km the factor is 11 → 1.0414 log10 → 1.4207 kcal/mol.

Put this in context and it becomes damning: 0.41 kcal/mol at the single most benign, most common assay condition already consumes over half of the 0.77 kcal/mol experimental noise floor that Ross/Kramer establish for public affinity data. And that is a BEST case — a known mechanism, a known Km, a single well-behaved competitive inhibitor. It is a systematic bias with a known sign (IC50 always overestimates Ki for competitive inhibition), not a random error that averages away.

For Huperzine A specifically: it is a reversible, mixed/competitive AChE inhibitor typically assayed by Ellman under substrate turnover. The single ChEMBL record this project pulled has standard_type = NULL, so it is not even known which of the six endpoint types it is. Comparing a pooled-referent model output to an unknown-referent database record and calling the difference an energy error compounds the category error on both sides. (This repository's own panel record separately notes 23 IC50 values for this pair spanning 3.99 log units, i.e. 5.4 kcal/mol of spread in the reference data alone — larger than the claimed 3.29 kcal/mol "error".)

=== 3. POOLING ===
The referent of the output is: a learned latent log-potency scale, calibrated to no single physical quantity, positioned by the mixture composition of the training corpus.

Concretely, the head was trained to place a Kd, a Ki, an IC50 at some unrecorded [S], an EC50 from an amplifying cell assay, an AC50 from an arbitrary HTS fit, and an XC50 of undeclared type ALL on the same axis. Those quantities differ from one another by assay-dependent multiplicative factors: (1 + [S]/Km) for IC50, an unbounded receptor-reserve factor for EC50, unspecified for AC50/XC50. On a log axis those become ADDITIVE OFFSETS. The model minimises a Huber loss weighted toward intra-assay pairwise differences, in which — as Boltz-2 says and Ross supports — those offsets cancel. In the absolute term they do not cancel; they are absorbed into a single fitted global intercept that represents the corpus-average offset and corresponds to nothing physical.

Therefore: NO. A pooled predictor's output cannot legitimately be converted to a thermodynamic state function. Not by any conversion, at any temperature, with any constant. A state function is defined by an equilibrium; this output is defined by a training-set mixture. There exists no function of the output alone that recovers ΔG°, because the information required — which endpoint type, under what [S], with what Km, by what mechanism — was discarded at label-construction time. This is not a calibration deficit that more data would close. It is an identifiability failure. You cannot invert a many-to-one map by choosing a better constant.

The one thing that IS licensed: within-assay differences, i.e. ΔΔ, for congeneric compounds scored under identical conditions. That is exactly what the loss was weighted for, exactly what Ross's ratio argument supports, and exactly what the FEP+ Pearson R = 0.66 benchmark measures (a per-assay correlation).

=== 4. THE 1.364 FACTOR ===
CONFIRMED. Computed this session from R = 8.314462618 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (NIST CODATA 2022, stated exact) with 1 thermochemical cal = 4.184 J: R = 1.987204×10⁻³ kcal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, RT(298.15 K) = 0.592485 kcal/mol, RT·ln(10) = 1.364247 kcal/mol. The docs' 1.364 is this to four significant figures. It also matches thermo.py's RT = 0.59248 exactly.

DIMENSIONALLY: legitimate. pIC50 is dimensionless; RT·ln(10) has units kcal/mol; the product has units kcal/mol. No dimensional analysis will ever flag this. That is precisely what makes it dangerous — the error is invisible to every automatic check the platform could run.

SEMANTICALLY: a category error, and I want to be exact about where the error enters. Multiplying a dimensionless log by RT·ln(10) is a valid unit conversion IF AND ONLY IF the log is the log of a standard equilibrium constant, because ΔG° = −RT ln K° (IUPAC Gold Book S05915: "K⚬ = e^(−Δ_rG⚬/RT)"). The operation is not "convert a number to kcal/mol"; it is "apply the thermodynamic relation ΔG° = −RT ln K°". That relation has a precondition: the argument must be an equilibrium constant. IC50 is not one. A pooled Ki/Kd/IC50/EC50/AC50/XC50 log-potency is emphatically not one.

So the multiplication silently asserts a premise it does not check. It converts a dimensionless number into kcal/mol correctly and asserts a thermodynamic identity falsely, in the same keystroke. Compare: multiplying a Likert score by RT·ln(10) also yields a number in kcal/mol. Dimensional consistency is necessary, never sufficient, and it is not evidence.

=== 5. THE RULING ===
"Never call it dG" is CORRECT. I considered the alternative seriously and reject it for this specific quantity.

The "apparent/effective ΔG with caveats" convention in the docking literature rests on a precondition that Boltz-2's affinity head does not satisfy. That convention arose for empirical scoring functions REGRESSED ONTO A SINGLE-REFERENT TARGET — Kd or Ki from PDBbind — where at least the label is a dissociation constant, so the output is a bad estimate of a well-defined quantity. Boltz-2's head is trained on six referents that are not the same quantity, with a loss weighted toward differences rather than levels, and with a fitted molecular-weight term in its ensembling. Its output is not a bad estimate of ΔG; it is an estimate of something else. "Apparent ΔG" describes accuracy; the defect here is identity. A caveat cannot repair an identity error, because the reader's model of "apparent ΔG" is "ΔG ± something", and that model is wrong in kind, not in width. This is the same reason this repository already refuses to write "binding free energy" next to a Vina score.

There is a second, independent reason to refuse the caveat: the sign. "Apparent ΔG" carries a sign convention. This quantity is sign-inverted relative to ΔG. A caveated "apparent ΔG = +8.04" is not a hedged claim; it is a wrong claim about the direction of a thermodynamic driving force, and it is exactly the value that disabled the platform's own implausibility guard.

WHERE THE PANEL WAS TOO WEAK — three extensions I would add:

(a) The prohibition is scoped to "binding free energy" / the dG name. The identical defect applies one level down, to Kd. A code path that writes 1274 nM from this head into a field named kd_molar or kd_nM, or that compares it to a ChEMBL Kd or Ki, commits the same category error and passes the existing build check. The rule must cover the whole equilibrium-constant family: ΔG, ΔG°, ΔΔG, Kd, Ka, Ki, pKd, pKi.

(b) The panel's reasoning leads with the sign. Sign is the weakest of the three arguments and the only reparable one. Re-rank: POOLED REFERENT first (fatal, irreparable), IC50 ≠ Kd second (systematic, quantifiable at 0.41 kcal/mol at [S]=Km), SIGN third (real, but a one-character fix that must not be mistaken for a remedy).

(c) The prohibition addresses the derived energy but not the absolute-value claim itself. Reporting "predicted IC50 = 1274 nM" as if it were a measured IC50 under stated conditions is the same error without the kcal/mol. The head's absolute level is not trusted by its own authors (per-assay mean-centred metrics) and an independent evaluation this session — Wan, Zhang, Xue & Coveney, arXiv:2603.05532, 16,780 compounds on 3CLPro and 21,702 on TNKS2 — concludes verbatim: "Energetic evaluations exhibit only weak to moderate correlations across the global datasets. Furthermore, a focused analysis of the top 100 compounds yields no significant correlation between the Boltz-2 predictions and the binding free energies from fine-grained ESMACS… while Boltz-2 offers substantial speed for initial screening, it lacks the energetic resolution required for lead identification."

WHAT THE PANEL GOT RIGHT AND SHOULD BE KEPT: the verify_all.py build-failing check on any code path converting affinity_pred_value into binding_free_energy is the correct enforcement mechanism, because the defect is dimensionally invisible and will otherwise be reintroduced by anyone who reads only the docs line. Extend its pattern list per (a).

ON THIS PARTICULAR RUN, two things the platform should be reporting instead of a free energy, both verified this session against runs/919fef2194e3/boltz_results_in_predictions_in_affinity_in.json:
- affinity_pred_value (0.10515692830085754) is the EXACT arithmetic mean of the two ensemble members (−0.2593143582344055 and 0.4696282148361206); equality holds to the last bit. The two members disagree by 0.7290 log10 units = 0.995 kcal/mol on the docs' own scale, on one input, from one model family. That intra-ensemble spread alone exceeds the 0.77 kcal/mol public-data noise floor and should be reported as the honest minimum uncertainty.
- affinity_probability_binary = 0.4447 — below 0.5, i.e. the binder/decoy head leans "not a binder" for a compound with measured nanomolar potency — and its two members straddle the decision boundary (0.5522 and 0.3372). This is the more informative and more damning number, and it is the one the docs actually recommend for hit discovery.

Finally: the run was single-sequence (msa: empty) with iptm = 0.7136 on the ligand interface. Boltz-2's own Limitations state, verbatim: "Boltz-2 relies on predicted 3D protein–ligand structures and reliable trunk features as input to the affinity module. If the model fails to identify the correct pocket or inaccurately reconstructs the binding interface or conformational state of the protein, downstream affinity predictions are unlikely to be reliable." An iptm of 0.71 on an interface produced without an MSA is not a regime in which any affinity number from this head should be reported as a point estimate at all.
permitted_usages: Report the raw field under its own name with its documented meaning attributed to the authors: 'Boltz-2 affinity_pred_value = 0.1052 (dimensionless; documented by the Boltz-2 authors as log10 of an IC50 expressed in µM)'. Naming the field and attributing the interpretation is honest; asserting the interpretation as fact is not.

Report affinity_probability_binary as the primary number for binder/decoy triage, which is what the Boltz documentation actually recommends: 'should be used to detect binders from decoys, for example in a hit-discovery stage.' On this run report 0.4447, and report that the two ensemble members straddle the 0.5 boundary at 0.5522 and 0.3372.

Use the head for RANKING within a congeneric series scored under one protocol — the within-assay use the loss was weighted for and the only use Ross et al. 2023's ratio argument supports. Report Spearman/Kendall rank agreement, never absolute values.

Report DIFFERENCES between two compounds scored identically, as a dimensionless Δlog10-potency, with an explicit statement that the shared assay-offset cancels in the difference and does not cancel in either term separately.

State the derived potency as an explicitly model-internal quantity with the arithmetic shown: 'Back-transforming the documented relation gives 10^0.1052 µM = 1.27 µM. This is the model's log-potency scale exponentiated, not a measured IC50 and not a dissociation constant.'

Quote the docs' conversion verbatim WITH its own label intact — 'the Boltz documentation gives (6 − y) × 1.364 as pIC50 in kcal/mol' — and note that 1.364 = RT·ln(10) = 1.364247 kcal/mol at 298.15 K, while stating that the quantity so produced is a rescaled log-potency and is sign-inverted relative to ΔG_bind°.

Report the intra-ensemble spread as the honest floor on uncertainty: members −0.2593 and 0.4696, a 0.7290 log10 spread (0.995 kcal/mol on the docs' scale) on a single input, which alone exceeds the 0.77–0.95 kcal/mol reproducibility floor of public affinity data (Kramer et al. 2012 as reported in Ross et al. 2023).
Use thermo.py's ΔG = RT·ln(Kd/c°) freely on genuine measured Kd or Ki values from a declared assay, with temperature and c° = 1 M stated — that path is correct and should stay.
State the negative result plainly: 'Boltz-2 emits no binding free energy. This platform reports none from this head.' A declared absence is a scientific result and should be surfaced, not hidden.
forbidden_usages: Calling affinity_pred_value, or anything derived from it, a binding free energy, ΔG, ΔG°, dG, free energy of binding, or binding energy — under any caveat, hedge, or qualifier.

Calling it an 'apparent', 'effective', 'estimated', 'predicted', 'pseudo-' or 'quasi-' ΔG. The docking-literature carve-out does not extend here: that convention presumes a single-referent Kd/Ki training target, which this head does not have. A caveat can widen an error bar; it cannot repair an identity error, and it cannot repair an inverted sign.
Writing the value into any field named binding_free_energy, dg, dg_kcal, delta_g, or any equivalent — the existing verify_all.py build-failing rule is correct and should be kept.

EXTENSION THE PRIOR PANEL MISSED: writing the exponentiated value into any field named kd, kd_molar, kd_nM, ka, ki, pkd, or pki, or comparing it to a database Kd/Ki as though like-for-like. The pooled-referent defect is identical one level down and currently passes the build check.

Passing the value to thermo.check(), kd_to_dg(), dg_to_kd(), or the REFERENCE_AFFINITIES plausibility table. Unflipped it is sign-inverted and the ΔG < −18.3 implausibility guard can never fire; flipped it is still not a ΔG, so the guard would be validating a quantity it was not written for.

Negating the sign and then calling the result ΔG. This is the specific false repair the panel's sign-first framing invites: it fixes the least important of the three defects and leaves the fatal one untouched.
Reporting the value as a measured or measurable IC50 under stated assay conditions. The training label was pooled across Ki/Kd/IC50/AC50/EC50/XC50; the output is not an IC50 at any [S].

Comparing it to a single ChEMBL record and reporting the gap as an energy error in kcal/mol. On this pair the reference record has standard_type = NULL — the endpoint type is unrecorded — so both sides of the comparison have undefined referents. The 3.29 kcal/mol figure is a difference between two quantities neither of which is a free energy.

Reporting both a ΔG and a Kd for the same candidate as if they were two independent results. At fixed T they are one degree of freedom related by ΔG° = RT·ln(Kd/c°); presenting both manufactures false corroboration from one number.

Writing any ΔG anywhere in the platform without an explicit standard state and temperature. Changing c° from 1 M to 1 mM shifts every binding free energy by RT·ln(1000) = +4.093 kcal/mol at 298.15 K with no physical change whatsoever; an undeclared standard state is an undeclared additive constant.

Reporting any point estimate from this head for a run whose interface confidence is weak. This run is single-sequence (msa: empty) with iptm = 0.7136, and the Boltz-2 paper states verbatim that where the model 'inaccurately reconstructs the binding interface or conformational state of the protein, downstream affinity predictions are unlikely to be reliable.'

Presenting dimensional consistency as evidence of correctness. Multiplying any dimensionless number by RT·ln(10) yields kcal/mol; the units check will never catch this error and must not be cited as though it had.

methods.name: Descriptor-range / bounding box (interpolation space)
methods.what_it_measures: Whether each descriptor value of the query lies within the per-descriptor min-max envelope of the training set. OECD calls this the model's 'interpolation space' or 'coverage'.
methods.equation: Inside iff min_j(X_train) <= x_qj <= max_j(X_train) for every descriptor j. OECD para 108 verbatim: 'The interpolation space of a one-descriptor model is simply the range between the minimum and the maximum value of that descriptor, as observed in the training set of the model.' OECD para 109 verbatim: 'The simplest method for describing the AD is to consider the ranges of the individual descriptors.'
methods.threshold_rule: Any single descriptor outside its training [min, max] => outside AD. OECD para 109 records two limitations verbatim: 'the AD may include internal empty spaces, i.e. interpolation regions where the relationship is not proved' and 'intercorrelation between the descriptors is not taken into account, unless the individual descriptors are replaced by their principal components'. It also assumes normality: 'This approach is based on the assumption that the descriptor values follow a normal distribution, and could therefore be unreliable if this assumption is violated.'
methods.source: OECD Guidance Document on the Validation of (Q)SAR Models, ENV/JM/MONO(2007)2, Chapter 4, paras 108-109 (PDF fetched from oecd.org this session, text extracted with pypdf).

methods.name: Leverage / hat matrix + Williams plot
methods.what_it_measures: Distance of the query from the centroid of the training descriptor space, in the metric induced by the training covariance (a Mahalanobis-type measure). OECD para 112: 'The leverage of a chemical provides a measure of the distance of the chemical from the centroid of its training set.'
methods.equation: h = (x_i^T (X^T X)^-1) x_i  -- transcribed verbatim from Khurshid et al.: 'The leverage, denoted as h, is computed using the "hat" matrix through the equation h = (x_i^T (X^T X)^-1) x_i), where X represents the matrix of the training set data points and x_i represents a specific data point for which the leverage is being calculated'. Diagonal entries of H are the training leverages; OECD para 112: 'Chemicals in the training set have leverage values between 0 and 1.'
methods.threshold_rule: OECD para 112 verbatim: 'A "warning leverage" (h*) is generally fixed at 3p/n, where n is the number of training chemicals, and p the number of descriptors plus one. A leverage value greater than the warning leverage is considered large.' NOTE ON NOTATION: OECD's 3p/n with p := (number of descriptors + 1) is algebraically identical to the form h* = 3(p+1)/n where p := number of descriptors. Both appear in the literature; they are the same rule, and the OECD wording is the one actually retrieved. Williams plot, OECD para 115 verbatim: 'a plot of standardised residuals (R) vs. leverages (or hat values, h), called the Williams graph'. Standard companion cutoff is +/-3 standardised residual units; the +/-3 figure was NOT RETRIEVED verbatim from the OECD document this session (OECD para 115 describes the plot but the retrieved text does not state the residual cutoff numerically).
methods.source: OECD ENV/JM/MONO(2007)2 paras 112-115 (fetched); equation transcribed from Khurshid, Loganathan & Duvinage, 'Comparative Evaluation of Applicability Domain Definition Methods for Regression Models', arXiv:2411.00920, section 2.0.2 (PDF fetched and extracted this session).

methods.name: k-nearest-neighbour distance to training set
methods.what_it_measures: Local density of training data around the query rather than distance to a global centroid. Khurshid et al. define a DA-Index family: 'kappa represents the distance of the test point to the kth-nearest neighbour in the training set. min-kappa represents the minimum distance from the test point to the k-nearest neighbours. gamma represents the mean distance of a test point to its k-nearest neighbours and delta corresponds to the length of the mean vector from a test point to its k-nearest neighbours.'
methods.equation: gamma(x_q) = (1/k) * sum over the k nearest training neighbours of d(x_q, x_(i)), with d = Euclidean distance on standardised descriptors and k = 5 (the setting stated by Khurshid et al.: 'This method is based on the K-NN approach. We used K=5 and Euclidean distance was used as a distance measure.'). Cosine variant transcribed verbatim as eq (1): cos(alpha_{xa,xb}) = sum_i(x_a,i * x_b,i) / sqrt(sum_i x_a,i^2 * sum_i x_b,i^2), converted to a dissimilarity via 1 - cos(alpha).
methods.threshold_rule: NO CANONICAL THRESHOLD EXISTS IN THE RETRIEVED SOURCES. Khurshid et al. state only: 'Predictions falling below a predefined AD threshold are considered within the domain. The threshold can be manually chosen.' The operational rule must therefore be declared by the platform, e.g. reject if gamma(x_q) exceeds the Qth percentile of the training set's own leave-one-out kNN distance distribution. I used Q=95 in the computation below; that choice is mine and is NOT derived from any retrieved source. This is exactly the kind of parameter that must be pre-registered rather than chosen after seeing the query.
methods.source: Khurshid et al., arXiv:2411.00920, section 2.0.2 (fetched). Empirical support that NN-similarity discriminates error: Sheridan, Feuston, Maiorov & Kearsley, J Chem Inf Comput Sci 2004, 44(6):1912-28, DOI 10.1021/ci049782w (abstract retrieved via PubMed this session).

methods.name: Convex hull
methods.what_it_measures: Whether the query lies inside the smallest convex region enclosing the training descriptor cloud - a tighter interpolation space than the axis-aligned bounding box.
methods.equation: NOT RETRIEVED as an explicit equation. OECD para 110 gives only a prose definition, verbatim: 'A more advanced method for defining the interpolation space of a model is to define the smallest convex area that contains the descriptors of the training set.' No formal membership test (e.g. linear-programming feasibility or half-space intersection form) was retrieved from any source this session.
methods.threshold_rule: Binary: inside the hull => in AD, outside => out. OECD para 110 records two limitations verbatim: 'this method does not solve completely the problem of empty spaces between the chemicals of the training set' and 'for models that contain many descriptors, the calculation of the convex area becomes a time-consuming computational problem'. The second limitation is decisive for a 200-descriptor model: exact convex-hull membership is computationally infeasible at that dimensionality, so this method is not practically available to the platform.

methods.name: Distance to centroid (Euclidean / Mahalanobis / Manhattan)
methods.what_it_measures: Geometric distance from the query to a single reference point in descriptor space, typically the training centroid.
methods.equation: NOT RETRIEVED. OECD para 111 names the family without giving formulae, verbatim: 'A different approach to defining the AD is based on a calculation of the distance between a query chemical and a defined point in the descriptor space of the model (typically, the centroid of the training set)... Different methods following this approach can be applied (e.g. Euclidean, Mahalanobis, Manhattan distance).' The explicit algebraic forms of the Euclidean, Mahalanobis and Manhattan distances were NOT retrieved from a source this session and are therefore not reproduced here.
methods.threshold_rule: NOT RETRIEVED as a numeric rule. OECD para 111 describes the mechanism qualitatively, verbatim: 'the advantage of the distance (also called geometric) approach is that confidence levels can be associated with the AD by drawing iso-distance contours in the interpolation space', with the stated disadvantage 'again the assumption of a normal distribution for the underlying data. This means that the contours are drawn solely on the basis of the distance from the centroid, and the population of the regions between two iso-distance contours is not taken into account.'

methods.name: Probability density estimation (parametric and non-parametric / KDE)
methods.what_it_measures: The estimated density of training data at the query point, rather than a distance. Handles internal voids and concave domain boundaries that range, distance and leverage methods miss.
methods.equation: NOT RETRIEVED. OECD para 116 describes the family verbatim - 'The most advanced statistical methods that are currently applied for identifying the (Q)SAR AD are probability density distribution-based methods. The probability density function of a data set can be estimated by parametric and non-parametric methods. The parametric methods assume a standard distribution (e.g. Gaussian or Poisson distribution) while the non-parametric methods (e.g. kernel density estimation function) make no assumptions about the data distribution' - but gives no kernel-density estimator formula. The KDE equation was NOT retrieved this session.
methods.threshold_rule: NOT RETRIEVED as a numeric rule. OECD para 116 states the qualitative trade-off verbatim: 'An advantage of non-parametric methods is the ability to identify internal empty spaces and, if necessary, to generate concave regions around the borders of the interpolation space to reflect the actual data distribution. It has been argued that the probability density approach is more robust than the range, distance and leverage approaches (Jaworska, 2005). However, it is also more restrictive in terms of the chemical space that falls in the AD of a model.'

methods.name: Ensemble standard deviation (deep-ensemble disagreement)
methods.what_it_measures: Spread of predictions across an ensemble, used as a proxy for epistemic uncertainty. Directly available for ADMET-AI, which already ensembles five models per endpoint.
methods.equation: Ensemble mean, Khurshid eq (3): F(f1(x), f2(x), ..., fn(x)) = (1/n) * sum_i f_i(x). Ensemble SD, Khurshid eq (4), transcribed exactly as printed in the fetched PDF: 'dstd(x) = F(x) = sqrt( sum_{i=1}^{N} (f_i(x) - F(x)) / (N-1) )'. TRANSCRIPTION FLAG: as printed in the source the summand lacks the square on (f_i(x) - F(x)) and the left-hand side redundantly repeats '= F(x)'; both are evidently typesetting errors in the source for the ordinary sample standard deviation. I reproduce the printed form rather than silently correcting it, per the accuracy contract.
methods.threshold_rule: No calibrated threshold. Khurshid et al. state only the direction: 'high AD values for a prediction mean low confidence and low AD values mean high confidence.' KNOWN FAILURE MODE, MEASURED: Ovadia et al. report verbatim as their first take-home message: 'Along with accuracy, the quality of uncertainty consistently degrades with increasing dataset shift regardless of method', and 'Better calibration and accuracy on the i.i.d. test dataset does not usually translate to better calibration under dataset shift (shifted versions as well as completely different OOD data).' Hirschfeld et al. (co-authored by Kyle Swanson, also an ADMET-AI author) report verbatim: 'No method consistently satisfied the objective of producing a strong ranking of errors, on either MPNNs or FFNs. Performance of this task was strongly dataset dependent, with all methods producing poor rankings for certain tasks.' Consequence: a SMALL ensemble SD far from the training data is not evidence of a reliable prediction.
methods.source: Khurshid et al. arXiv:2411.00920 eqs (2)-(4); Ovadia et al., 'Can You Trust Your Model's Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift', NeurIPS 2019, arXiv:1906.02530, section 5; Hirschfeld, Swanson, Yang, Barzilay & Coley, 'Uncertainty Quantification using Neural Networks for Molecular Property Prediction', arXiv:2005.10036. All three PDFs fetched and text-extracted this session.

methods.name: Gaussian-process posterior variance
methods.what_it_measures: Bayesian posterior predictive variance under a GP prior, which grows away from training data by construction of the kernel.
methods.equation: NOT RETRIEVED. Khurshid et al. describe the method in prose only - 'The predictions of GPR are represented by a Gaussian distribution, characterized by a mean and a covariance' - and note the hyperparameters: 'alpha, which stands for the noise level (also acts as a regularization of the model), the parameter gamma of the RBF kernel which represents the covariance function, and variance threshold sigma*'. The closed-form GP posterior variance expression was NOT retrieved from any source this session and is therefore not reproduced.
methods.threshold_rule: A variance threshold sigma* chosen by the user (named but not numerically specified in the retrieved source). Same failure mode as ensemble variance: the guarantee is conditional on the kernel being correct, which is precisely what is unverifiable far from the data. Ovadia et al.'s measured finding that uncertainty quality 'consistently degrades with increasing dataset shift regardless of method' applies to Bayesian methods too - their benchmark explicitly covers Bayesian and non-Bayesian approaches.
methods.source: Khurshid et al. arXiv:2411.00920, section 2.0.3 (fetched); Ovadia et al. arXiv:1906.02530 (fetched).

methods.name: Split / inductive conformal prediction
methods.what_it_measures: Converts any point predictor into a set/interval predictor with a finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantee. This is the one framework that turns a refusal into a calibrated statement.
methods.equation: Nonconformity scores, Xu et al. verbatim: homoscedastic 'alpha = |y - y_hat|'; heteroscedastic, their eq (1), 'alpha = |y - y_hat| / sigma(X)' where 'sigma(X) is an estimate of the accuracy of the point predictor'. Calibration quantile, Angelopoulos & Bates verbatim: 'define q_hat to be the ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n empirical quantile of s_1, ..., s_n, where ceil is the ceiling function (q_hat is essentially the 1-alpha quantile, but with a small correction)'. Prediction set: C(X) = {y : s(X, y) <= q_hat}. For regression, Xu et al.: 'The prediction interval for a new molecule x_new in the test set would be: y_hat(x_new) +/- alpha_theta * sigma(x_new)'.
methods.threshold_rule: THE GUARANTEE, verbatim from Angelopoulos & Bates eq (1): '1 - alpha <= P(Y_test in C(X_test)) <= 1 - alpha + 1/(n+1)'. They define the term verbatim: 'the probability that the prediction set contains the correct label is almost exactly 1 - alpha; we call this property MARGINAL COVERAGE, since the probability is marginal (averaged) over the randomness in the calibration and test points.' Formal statement, Theorem D.1: 'Suppose (X_i, Y_i)_{i=1..n} and (X_test, Y_test) are i.i.d. Then define q_hat as q_hat = inf{q : |{i : s(X_i,Y_i) <= q}|/n >= ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n} and the resulting prediction sets as C(X) = {y : s(X,y) <= q_hat}. Then P(Y_test in C(X_test)) >= 1 - alpha.' They add verbatim: 'the theorem also holds if the observations satisfy the weaker condition of exchangeability'. Xu et al. add verbatim: 'This marginal validity property does not depend on any distributional assumptions or model assumptions, and holds for any sample data size.' CRITICAL LIMIT: marginal is NOT per-molecule. Xu et al. verbatim: 'Marginal, is roughly understood as averaged over all molecules', and on the stronger property, 'Compared to marginal validity, conditional validity is a much more stringent requirement usually impossible to achieve.'
methods.source: Angelopoulos & Bates, 'A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification', arXiv:2107.07511v6, eq (1), Figure 2, Theorem D.1; Xu, Liaw, Sheridan & Svetnik, 'Development and Evaluation of Conformal Prediction Methods for QSAR', arXiv:2304.00970, section 3.1. Both PDFs fetched and extracted this session. Originating QSAR application: Norinder, Carlsson, Boyer & Eklund, J Chem Inf Model 2014, 54:1596-1603, DOI 10.1021/ci5001168 (title and citation confirmed by search this session; full text NOT retrieved).

methods.name: Mondrian / class-conditional / group-balanced conformal prediction
methods.what_it_measures: Restores coverage WITHIN declared categories, instead of only on average across the whole test distribution. This is what stops a model from paying for its errors on hard molecules with easy ones.
methods.equation: Mondrian taxonomy, Fontana/Zeni/Vantini verbatim: 'a measurable function kappa maps each z to its category k, belonging to the (usually finite) measurable space K of all categories... Such a function kappa is called a Mondrian taxonomy, as a tribute to the Dutch painter Piet Mondrian.' Mondrian p-value, their eq (3.7) verbatim: 'p_z := |{i = 1,...,n+1 : kappa_i = kappa_{n+1} & R_i >= R_{n+1}}| / |{i = 1,...,n+1 : kappa_i = kappa_{n+1}}|, where kappa_{n+1} = kappa(z)'. Equivalent per-group quantile form, Angelopoulos & Bates: q_hat(g) = Quantile(s_1,...,s_{n(g)} ; ceil((n(g)+1)(1-alpha)) / n(g)), 'where n(g) is the number of examples of group g', with C(x) = {y : s(x,y) <= q_hat(x_1)}.
methods.threshold_rule: GUARANTEE ADDED, group-balanced, Angelopoulos & Bates eq (8) verbatim: 'P(Y_test in C(X_test) | X_test,1 = g) >= 1 - alpha, for all groups g in {1,...,G}'; class-conditional, their eq (9): 'P(Y_test in C(X_test) | Y_test = y) >= 1 - alpha, for all classes y in {1,...,K}'. They state the motivation verbatim: 'Recall that a standard application of conformal prediction will not necessarily yield coverage within each group simultaneously... the marginal guarantee from normal conformal prediction can still be satisfied even if all errors happen in one group.' Vovk-lineage statement, Fontana et al.: 'A stronger kind of validity, validity within categories, which is especially relevant in the situation of asymmetric classification, is the main property of Mondrian conformal predictors (MCPs), first introduced in Vovk et al. (2003).' HARD REQUIREMENT: a category only gets a guarantee if it contains calibration examples - n(g) must be non-zero. A molecular-weight bin containing zero calibration molecules gets no Mondrian guarantee at all. This is the precise reason Mondrian conformal does NOT rescue the 4943 Da case.
methods.source: Fontana, Zeni & Vantini, 'Conformal Prediction: a Unified Review of Theory and New Challenges', arXiv:2005.07972, sections 3.1 and 3.1.1, eqs (3.3) and (3.7), Proposition 3.1; Angelopoulos & Bates arXiv:2107.07511 sections 4.1-4.2, eqs (8)-(9), Propositions 1-2. Both fetched this session. Original: Vovk, Lindsay, Nouretdinov & Gammerman (2003), cited therein, NOT directly retrieved. QSAR application: Sun/Norinder et al., 'Applying Mondrian Cross-Conformal Prediction To Estimate Prediction Confidence on Large Imbalanced Bioactivity Data Sets', J Chem Inf Model 2017, DOI 10.1021/acs.jcim.7b00159 (citation confirmed by search; full text NOT retrieved).

methods.name: Conformal outlier detection (calibrated applicability domain)
methods.what_it_measures: THE KEY CONSTRUCTION FOR THIS DISPUTE. Turns an AD score into a refusal rule with a guaranteed false-refusal rate, using only unlabelled training-distribution data. It makes 'I refuse' falsifiable, which is exactly what the reviewer demanded.
methods.equation: Angelopoulos & Bates, section 4.4, verbatim: 'we will construct a function that labels test points as outliers or inliers, C : X -> {outlier, inlier}'. Score s : X -> R depends on features only (unsupervised). Compute s_i = s(X_i) on clean data, then 'q_hat = quantile(s_1, ..., s_n; ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n)'. Decision rule verbatim: 'C(x) = inlier if s(x) <= q_hat, outlier if s(x) > q_hat.'
methods.threshold_rule: GUARANTEE, their eq (14) verbatim: 'P(C(X_test) = outlier) <= alpha, where the probability is over X_test, a fresh sample from the clean-data distribution.' In platform terms: the probability of refusing a genuinely in-domain molecule is at most alpha. Setting alpha = 0.01 means the platform provably refuses at most 1% of molecules drawn from its own training distribution - a directly checkable, falsifiable claim that distinguishes a calibrated refusal from an off-switch. Any AD score (kNN distance, leverage, ensemble SD) can be plugged in as s.
methods.source: Angelopoulos & Bates, arXiv:2107.07511, section 4.4, eq (14) and Proposition 3 (fetched this session).

methods.name: Conformal prediction under covariate shift (weighted conformal)
methods.what_it_measures: Restores coverage when the test distribution differs from training, by reweighting calibration scores with the density ratio. Determines whether conformal can be salvaged for an out-of-distribution query.
methods.equation: Angelopoulos & Bates, section 4.5, verbatim: weights w(x) 'usually this is just the ratio of the new PDF to the old PDF at the point x', with p^w_i(x) = w(X_i) / (sum_j w(X_j) + w(x)) and p^w_test(x) = w(x) / (sum_j w(X_j) + w(x)). Shifted quantile: 'q_hat(x) = inf{ s_j : sum_{i=1}^{j} p^w_i(x) * 1{s_i <= s_j} >= 1 - alpha }', then C(x) = {y : s(x,y) <= q_hat(x)}.
methods.threshold_rule: Theorem 3 verbatim: 'Suppose (X_1,Y_1),...,(X_n,Y_n) are drawn i.i.d. from P x P_{Y|X} and that (X_test, Y_test) is drawn independently from P_test x P_{Y|X}. Then the choice of C above satisfies P(Y_test in C(X_test)) >= 1 - alpha.' DECISIVE LIMITATION FOR THIS CASE: the guarantee requires a KNOWN density ratio. The authors state verbatim: 'This algorithm addresses a somewhat restricted case - that of a known covariate shift'. Where the training density is zero (no molecules of that class at all), w(x) = p_test(x)/p_train(x) is a division by zero and is not estimable, so this theorem provides no coverage for the query in question.
methods.source: Angelopoulos & Bates, arXiv:2107.07511, section 4.5, Theorem 3 (fetched this session).

methods.name: IMPOSSIBILITY RESULT: distribution-free object-conditional coverage
methods.what_it_measures: Not an AD method - the theorem that bounds what any AD or uncertainty method can promise for a single named molecule. It is the reason a per-molecule guarantee cannot be manufactured for the 4943 Da candidate.
methods.equation: Fontana/Zeni/Vantini, eq (3.2), verbatim: 'distribution-free conditional coverage, that is: P(Y_{n+1} in Gamma_alpha(x) | X_{n+1} = x) >= 1 - alpha for all P and a.a. x, with Gamma_alpha(x) = Gamma_alpha(Z_1,...,Z_n,x) is impossible to achieve with a finite sample for rich object spaces, such as X = R (Lei and Wasserman (2014), Lemma 1).' Intermediate notion, their eq (3.3) local validity: 'P(Y_{n+1} in Gamma_alpha(X_{n+1}) | X_{n+1} in A_j) >= 1 - alpha for all j and all P', given a partition A = {A_j : j >= 1} of supp(P_X).
methods.threshold_rule: Consequence, verbatim: 'the requirement of precise object conditional validity cannot be satisfied in a nontrivial way, unless we know the true probability distribution generating the data... or unless the test object is an atom of the data-generating distribution. If we impose that requirement, the prediction interval is expected to have infinite length (Vovk (2012)...).' PRACTICAL READING: no method can hand you a finite, guaranteed interval for one specific molecule without extra assumptions. The achievable middle ground is LOCAL validity over a partition cell - which requires the cell to contain calibration data. A cell defined as 'MW > 3000 Da and charge >= +9' contains zero TDC calibration molecules (measured below), so even local validity is unavailable.
methods.source: Fontana, Zeni & Vantini, arXiv:2005.07972, section 3.1, eqs (3.2)-(3.3), citing Lei & Wasserman (2014) Lemma 1 and Vovk (2012) (fetched this session; the Lei & Wasserman and Vovk originals were NOT directly retrieved).

methods.name: EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE: do AD measures actually correlate with observed error?
methods.what_it_measures: Whether the whole AD enterprise delivers. Mixed, with important negative results - this is the literature that makes a composition-only refusal insufficient in the general case.
methods.equation: Not an equation. Key measured findings, transcribed from retrieved sources. POSITIVE (Sheridan 2004, abstract via PubMed): 'the similarity of the molecule to be predicted to the nearest molecule in the training set and/or the number of neighbors in the training set' are useful; 'The molecules with the highest similarity and/or the most neighbors are the best-predicted. This trend holds true for narrow training sets and, to a lesser degree, for many diverse training sets and does not depend on which QSAR method or descriptor is used.' QUALIFIED (Sheridan 2015, abstract via PubMed): the useful metrics change with training-set diversity - 'when data sets are less diverse... these two DA metrics become less important in explaining prediction error, and the DA metric SIMILARITYNEAREST1... becomes more important', with the operational recommendation keyed to 'when the mean pairwise similarity (measured with the Carhart AP descriptor and the Dice similarity index) within a QSAR training set is less than 0.5'.
methods.threshold_rule: NEGATIVE RESULTS. (i) Khurshid et al. state the correlation is only aggregate, verbatim: 'It should be clearly stated that prediction accuracy correlates with AD measure only on average: for example, data points in the range [0.1, 0.3] generally exhibit higher prediction accuracy than those in the range [0.6, 0.7]. However, individual data points within the first interval may still have larger prediction errors than some data points within the second interval.' (ii) Mora et al. 2024 (abstract via PubMed) is the strongest negative: 'the applicability domain (AD) estimation has been recognized in several reports in the literature to be one of the most challenging, implying that the actual reliability measures of model predictions are often unreliable', and their measured result across 5 QSAR models: 'predictions erroneously tagged as reliable (AD prediction errors) overwhelmingly correspond to instances in subspaces (cohorts) with the highest prediction error rates, highlighting the inhomogeneity of the AD space.' They call verbatim 'for more stringent AD analysis guidelines which require the incorporation of model error analysis schemes' and insist 'any selected AD method should be rigorously validated to demonstrate its suitability for the model space over which it is applied.' (iii) OECD para 100 anticipated this verbatim: 'it should not automatically be assumed that all predictions within the defined AD are necessarily reliable.' (iv) OECD para 114 states the converse asymmetry verbatim: 'While the observation that a chemical has a large leverage indicates that it is outside the descriptor coverage of the model, a chemical with small leverage can also be outside the AD for other reasons.' NOTE: a widely-quoted figure of SRCC 0.14-0.38 for distance-to-training vs model variance surfaced in search snippets this session but I could NOT retrieve its primary source, so it is recorded here as NOT RETRIEVED and is not relied upon.
methods.source: Sheridan et al. 2004, DOI 10.1021/ci049782w; Sheridan 2015, J Chem Inf Model 55(6):1098-107, DOI 10.1021/acs.jcim.5b00110; Mora et al., 'Rethinking the applicability domain analysis in QSAR models', J Comput Aided Mol Des 2024, 38(1):9, DOI 10.1007/s10822-024-00550-8 - all three abstracts retrieved via PubMed this session (full texts NOT retrieved); Khurshid et al. arXiv:2411.00920 section 2.0.1 (full PDF fetched); OECD ENV/JM/MONO(2007)2 paras 100 and 114 (fetched).

applicability_domain.the_criterion:
THE CRITERION (the decision rule separating principled refusal from evasion)

A refusal is SCIENTIFICALLY JUSTIFIED if and only if all four conditions hold. Fail any one and it is an evasion.

C1. DEFINED IN ADVANCE. There exists a written, version-pinned membership function A(x) -> R with a fixed threshold t, specifying: the exact descriptor set, the standardisation, the reference training set (with a content hash and molecule count), and t. Pre-registered means fixed before the query is seen. This is OECD Principle 3 operationalised - OECD para 98 verbatim: "Ideally, the AD should be defined and documented by the model developer. This information should include: a statement of the unambiguous model algorithm..., details of the training set (chemical identification, descriptors and endpoint values), details of the (statistical) method to derive the model, and structural requirements determined during model development." OECD para 98 also requires it be per-model: "every model should be associated with its own AD".

C2. NON-VACUOUS, AND DEMONSTRATED TO BE SO. The platform must publish the ACCEPTANCE RATE of A on a held-out reference set it did not tune on. This is the direct answer to the reviewer. "A platform that can only ever refuse has not been distinguished from a platform that cannot compute" is a claim about the acceptance region being empty - and an empty acceptance region is an empirical property that can be measured and reported. A refusal rule that admits, say, 96% of a druglike held-out set and rejects this peptide has been distinguished from an off-switch. A refusal rule whose acceptance rate has never been computed has not. Preferred implementation: conformal outlier detection, which converts C2 from a courtesy into a theorem - Angelopoulos & Bates eq (14), P(C(X_test) = outlier) <= alpha over the clean-data distribution, i.e. a provable ceiling on the false-refusal rate.

C3. MEASURED ON THIS QUERY, AS A NUMBER. The platform must emit A(x), t, and the ratio - not a verdict, not a category. "MW 4910 Da exceeds 1000 Da" is a restatement of the rule. "leverage h = 0.1417 against warning leverage h* = 0.001177, a factor of 120" is a measurement.

C4. THE STATED GROUND MUST BE THE ACTUAL GROUND. The reason given to the user must be the quantity that actually triggered the rejection. If the platform says "molecular weight" but the descriptor that fell outside the training envelope was hydrogen-bond-donor count, the explanation is false even though the decision is right.

WHEN IS A MEASURED ERROR CURVE REQUIRED, AND WHEN IS COMPOSITION ENOUGH?

This is the crux, and the answer is a clean dichotomy on TRAINING SUPPORT:

- ZERO SUPPORT (no training molecules in the region at all): composition alone is sufficient and an error curve is NOT required, because an error curve is not merely unavailable - it is undefined. Error is measured against labels; where there are no labelled molecules there is nothing to measure. Demanding an error curve in a zero-support region is demanding that the platform manufacture data. The absence of data IS the finding. BUT the zero support must be MEASURED AND REPORTED (a count, from a named dataset), not asserted from the general character of the training corpus. The difference between case (a) and case (c) here is entirely the difference between a counted zero and an assumed zero.

- SPARSE BUT NON-ZERO SUPPORT: composition is NOT sufficient. Here an error curve is both possible and mandatory, because the model may well extrapolate acceptably, and refusing without measuring throws away real capability. Mora et al. 2024 is the governing negative result: AD labels are themselves unreliable, and "predictions erroneously tagged as reliable... overwhelmingly correspond to instances in subspaces (cohorts) with the highest prediction error rates". In the sparse regime you must bin by the AD score and report observed error per bin.

THE THREE CASES AND THEIR EVIDENCE REQUIREMENTS

(a) PRINCIPLED REFUSAL - the AD is defined and the query is measurably outside it.
Evidence required: C1-C4 satisfied; at least one AD function with a pre-registered threshold reports the query outside, with the numeric margin stated; the training-support count in the query's region reported (and, if zero, stated as a counted zero from a named, hashed dataset); the acceptance rate of the same rule on a held-out reference set published to prove non-vacuity; and the refusal calibrated so P(refuse | in-distribution) <= alpha. Additionally, because different AD metrics disagree (see the ruling), the platform must report the FULL PANEL, including any metric that does NOT flag the query. Reporting only the metrics that agree with the decision is selective evidence.

(b) PRINCIPLED PREDICTION WITH A WIDENED INTERVAL - inside the AD but far from the centre.
Evidence required: query inside the AD by the pre-registered rule but in a high-AD-score bin; a labelled calibration set drawn from the same distribution; split conformal with a heteroscedastic nonconformity score alpha = |y - y_hat| / sigma(X) (Xu et al. eq 1) so the interval widens where the model is locally uncertain; the quantile taken at ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n; AND - this is the part usually skipped - MONDRIAN conformal with the taxonomy defined by the AD-score bin, so coverage holds within the far-from-centre bin rather than only on average. Plain marginal coverage is inadequate here precisely because, as Angelopoulos & Bates note, "the marginal guarantee from normal conformal prediction can still be satisfied even if all errors happen in one group". Report empirical coverage per bin on held-out data. The bin must contain calibration molecules; if n(g) = 0 the guarantee does not exist and the case is (a), not (b).

(c) EVASION - refusal with no defined AD and no measurement.
Diagnostic signature, any one of: no A written down; A written down but never evaluated on the query; no acceptance rate ever computed, so the rule cannot be shown to admit anything; a threshold chosen after seeing the query; the stated ground differing from the computed ground; or a refusal that generalises to a whole class ("peptides") without a per-query number. The tell is that nothing about the output could change based on a computation - the refusal is entailed by the policy rather than by the molecule.

WHAT NO AMOUNT OF MACHINERY CAN BUY. Distribution-free object-conditional coverage is impossible (Fontana et al. eq 3.2, citing Lei & Wasserman Lemma 1): "the requirement of precise object conditional validity cannot be satisfied in a nontrivial way... If we impose that requirement, the prediction interval is expected to have infinite length." So the honest ceiling on any per-molecule claim is local/Mondrian validity over a populated cell. No conformal wrapper converts a zero-support region into a valid finite interval - and covariate-shift conformal (Theorem 3) needs a known density ratio w(x) = p_test/p_train, which is a division by zero when training density is zero.
applicability_domain.is_current_refusal_justified:
RULING: The refusal reaches the RIGHT OUTCOME for the WRONG STATED REASON, and until this session it was formally case (c) - an evasion - because the number that justifies it had never been computed. It is now case (a), but only because I measured it. The reviewer was substantively correct about the epistemics and incorrect about the conclusion.

WHAT I MEASURED THIS SESSION (all numbers computed here, reproducible; scripts in the implementation field)

Reference set: 16 TDC ADMET datasets downloaded directly from Harvard Dataverse (IDs from tdc/metadata.py name2id), parsed with RDKit 2026.03.5 -> 53,525 valid molecules. Note ADMET-AI trains on 41 TDC datasets; I retrieved 16, so these are a substantial but not complete sample of its training space.

Molecular weight, pooled: median 305.3 Da; p90 478.6; p99 781.7; p99.9 1450.3; p99.99 2285.7; max 5299.5 Da.
  - > 1000 Da: 224 molecules (0.42%)
  - > 2000 Da: 11 (0.021%)
  - > 3000 Da: 1 (0.0019%)
CRITICAL REFINEMENT: that single >3000 Da entry is a multi-component SMILES (a salt/mixture). Splitting into covalent fragments and taking the largest, THE HEAVIEST SINGLE COVALENT MOLECULE IN THE ENTIRE 53,525-MOLECULE SPACE IS 2285.7 Da. Zero single molecules above 3000 Da. The candidate at 4943 Da is 2.16x the heaviest single species the model has ever seen.

Formal charge, pooled: 97.19% neutral; max observed +5 (one molecule); only 5 molecules at charge >= +4; ZERO molecules at charge >= +9. Joint constraint MW > 2000 Da AND charge >= +4: ZERO molecules.

So the composition claim, previously asserted, is now COUNTED. On the charge axis the support is exactly zero, not merely sparse.

AD PANEL, run against a constructed proxy polycationic peptide (43 residues, MW 4910.2 Da - matched to the candidate's 4943 Da; I did not have the real structure, and my proxy carries ~+19 rather than +9, so the charge-axis conclusions below rest on the TRAINING-SET counts, which are proxy-independent, not on the proxy's own charge):

  [1] Bounding box, 20 documented physicochemical descriptors: 7 of 20 OUTSIDE the training min-max envelope - TPSA (2082.9 vs max 1214.3), HBD (80 vs 27), RotB (184 vs 141), NumN (78 vs 32), AmideBonds (42 vs 20), NHOHCount (100 vs 66), NOCount (123 vs 89). VERDICT: OUTSIDE.
  [2] Leverage: h = 0.1417 against warning leverage h* = 3(p+1)/n = 3(21)/53525 = 0.001177. Ratio 120x. Training median leverage 0.00020, p99 0.0025. VERDICT: OUTSIDE (Williams-plot high-leverage extrapolation).
  [3] kNN distance (k=5, standardised Euclidean): 97.91 against a 95th-percentile training threshold of 1.623 - 60x the threshold, and 1.33x beyond the LARGEST kNN distance of any training molecule (73.58). VERDICT: OUTSIDE.
  [4] Nearest-neighbour Tanimoto (Morgan r=2, 2048 bit) against all 53,525: max similarity 0.595. VERDICT: NOT OUTSIDE. 23.6% of training molecules are MORE isolated from their own nearest neighbour than this peptide is.

THE THREE FINDINGS THAT DECIDE THE RULING

1. THE STATED GROUND IS NOT THE ACTUAL GROUND - the "MW > 1000 Da" rule fails criterion C4. MW 4910 Da is INSIDE the raw MW bounding box (training max 5299.5 Da), so a naive descriptor-range test on molecular weight alone does NOT reject this molecule. Molecular weight is not what places it outside the domain; hydrogen-bonding capacity, amide count, nitrogen count, TPSA, leverage and local density are. The 1000 Da cutoff is simultaneously over-inclusive (it would refuse the 224 training molecules above 1000 Da that the model was actually fitted on, and on which its reported performance partly rests) and under-motivated (it is a round number, not a boundary derived from the training set). A hard rule at a round number is a policy, not an applicability domain.

2. THE AD METRICS DISAGREE, WHICH IS WHY "DEFINED" IS NOT OPTIONAL. Fingerprint similarity does not flag this molecule; descriptor-geometry does. A peptide is locally familiar and globally alien - built from amide bonds and aliphatic side chains that appear throughout the training set, which is exactly what Morgan fingerprints see, while being far outside the training envelope in every size- and polarity-extensive property.
